instruments.short_name: Indian Contract Act: guarantee, indemnity, pledge, lien
instruments.title: Indian Contract Act, 1872: contracts of indemnity and guarantee (ss. 124-147), bailment, bankers' lien and pledge (ss. 148-181), and related general provisions
applies_to: Every lender taking a guarantee, an indemnity or a pledge of goods, shares or other movables
Guarantors (sureties), pawnors and borrowers
Banks, as holders of the general lien in s. 171
key_concepts: Contract of indemnity: a promise to save the other party from loss caused by the promisor or any other person (s. 124); rights of the indemnity-holder when sued (s. 125)

Contract of guarantee: a promise to perform the promise or discharge the liability of a third person on default; the parties are the surety, the principal debtor and the creditor; it may be oral or written (s. 126)
Co-extensive liability: the surety is liable to the same extent as the principal debtor unless the contract says otherwise (s. 128)

Continuing guarantee: one that extends to a series of transactions (s. 129); it may be revoked as to future transactions by notice (s. 130) and is revoked as to future transactions by the surety's death, unless the contract says otherwise (s. 131)

Discharge of the surety: by a variance in the terms made without the surety's consent (s. 133); by a release or discharge of the principal debtor (s. 134); by a composition, a promise to give time or a promise not to sue made with the principal debtor without the surety's assent (s. 135); by an act or omission of the creditor that impairs the surety's eventual remedy (s. 139); and to the extent of the value of any security the creditor loses or gives up without the surety's consent (s. 141)
Rights of a surety who pays: subrogation to all the creditor's rights against the principal debtor (s. 140) and the benefit of every security the creditor held when the guarantee was given (s. 141)
Bankers' general lien: bankers may retain goods bailed to them as security for a general balance of account, unless the contract says otherwise (s. 171)
Pledge: the bailment of goods as security for a debt or the performance of a promise; the bailor is the pawnor and the bailee the pawnee (s. 172)

Penalty clauses: where a contract names a sum or a penalty for breach, only reasonable compensation up to that sum is recoverable; a stipulation for increased interest from the date of default may be a penalty (s. 74 and Explanation)

Agreements that limit the time to enforce rights, or extinguish rights on the expiry of a specified period, are void to that extent (s. 28). Exception 3 saves a written guarantee by a bank or a financial institution that ends liability after a period of at least one year from a specified event; 'bank' and 'financial institution' (a public financial institution) are defined narrowly in the Explanation, so most NBFCs and HFCs are not covered
core_obligations: s. 176: on the pawnor's default the pawnee may sue on the debt and keep the goods as collateral, or sell the goods after giving the pawnor reasonable notice of the sale; any shortfall remains payable and any surplus must be paid to the pawnor
s. 177: a defaulting pawnor may redeem the goods at any time before their actual sale, paying the expenses caused by the default

s. 173-174: the pawnee may retain the goods for the debt, interest and necessary expenses, but not for any other debt unless the contract says so; such a contract is presumed for subsequent advances by the pawnee
s. 133, 135 and 141: obtain the surety's consent before varying the loan terms, giving the borrower time or a composition, or releasing or losing any security, or the surety may be discharged
s. 130: a continuing guarantee may be revoked by the surety for future transactions by notice to the creditor; past liabilities survive
s. 137: mere forbearance to sue the borrower does not discharge the surety, unless the guarantee says otherwise; a binding agreement to give time does (s. 135)
consequences_stated: s. 133: a variance without the surety's consent discharges the surety as to transactions after the variance; ss. 134, 135 and 139: release of the debtor, a binding promise to give time or not to sue, or an act impairing the surety's remedy discharges the surety; s. 141: losing or parting with security discharges the surety to the value of that security
s. 74: a lender can recover only reasonable compensation, not the full stipulated penalty, for breach; higher default interest may be treated as a penalty
s. 28: a clause cutting down the time to sue is void to that extent, except within Exception 3

instruments.short_name: Sale of Goods Act: title to goods financed
instruments.title: Sale of Goods Act, 1930: passing of property, transfer of title and the unpaid seller's rights
applies_to: Lenders financing or taking security over goods: vehicles, equipment, inventory and receivables from goods sold
Buyers and sellers of goods, including borrowers who buy goods with borrowed money
key_concepts: Property passes when the parties intend it to pass, judged from the contract, the parties' conduct and the circumstances (s. 19); for specific goods in a deliverable state it passes when the contract is made, even if payment or delivery is postponed (s. 20)
For unascertained or future goods, property passes when goods of the contract description are unconditionally appropriated to the contract (s. 23)

Nemo dat: a buyer from a person who is not the owner gets no better title than the seller had, except where the owner's conduct precludes him, or a mercantile agent in possession with the owner's consent sells in the ordinary course of business to a buyer in good faith (s. 27)
A buyer in good faith from a seller holding under a voidable contract that has not been rescinded gets good title (s. 29)
A seller or buyer left in possession of goods or documents of title can pass good title, including by pledge, to a person taking in good faith without notice (s. 30)
Unpaid seller: one who has not been paid or tendered the whole price, or whose negotiable instrument taken as conditional payment was dishonoured (s. 45)
core_obligations: s. 46-47: the unpaid seller keeps a lien on goods in his possession for the price, a right of stoppage in transit on the buyer's insolvency and a limited right of resale, even after property has passed; a financier of the buyer generally takes subject to these rights (s. 53(1)), except that a good-faith pledgee for value of a document of title takes free of the lien and stoppage to the extent of its rights (s. 53(1) proviso)

s. 27 and 30: before lending against goods, confirm the borrower's title and possession; a pledge from a person who is not the owner binds the owner only in the cases the law allows, such as s. 30 here and Contract Act ss. 178 (mercantile agent) and 178A (possession under a voidable contract)
consequences_stated: s. 27: a lender taking goods from a non-owner, outside the exceptions, takes no better title than the borrower had

instruments.short_name: Transfer of Property Act: mortgages, charges, assignment of debts
instruments.title: Transfer of Property Act, 1882: mortgages and charges of immovable property (ss. 58-104) and transfer of actionable claims (ss. 130-137)
instruments.theme: Mortgages, property and goods as security
applies_to: Lenders taking a mortgage or charge over land or buildings, including home loans and loans against property
Mortgagors, sureties and later purchasers or lenders over the same property
Lenders buying or selling loan receivables (assignment of actionable claims)
key_concepts: Mortgage: the transfer of an interest in specific immovable property to secure money advanced or to be advanced, an existing or future debt, or an engagement that may give rise to a pecuniary liability (s. 58(a))
Kinds of mortgage: simple (s. 58(b)), by conditional sale (s. 58(c)), usufructuary (s. 58(d)), English (s. 58(e)), by deposit of title-deeds in the notified towns (s. 58(f)) and anomalous (s. 58(g))

Form: where the principal money is Rs 100 or more, a mortgage other than one by deposit of title-deeds can be made only by a registered instrument signed by the mortgagor and attested by at least two witnesses (s. 59)
Right to redeem: once the principal is due, the mortgagor may pay and require return of the title documents, re-delivery of possession and a re-transfer or acknowledgement (s. 60)
Charge: where immovable property is made security by act of parties or operation of law without amounting to a mortgage; the rules for simple mortgages apply so far as may be (s. 100)
Priority: later rights over the same property are subject to earlier rights, absent a special contract (s. 48)

Assignment of unsecured debts: an actionable claim (a debt not secured by a mortgage of immovable property or by hypothecation or pledge of movables, s. 3) is transferred by a signed written instrument; the transfer is complete on execution and the transferee may sue in its own name, but the debtor's dealings with the transferor stay valid until the debtor has express notice (ss. 130-131); the transferee takes subject to the transferor's liabilities and equities, such as set-off (s. 132)
core_obligations: s. 59: register and attest every mortgage deed where the principal is Rs 100 or more, unless it is a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds

s. 67 and 67A: a mortgagee enforces through a suit for sale or foreclosure once the money is due, and must sue on all mortgages from the same mortgagor on which money has become due, absent a contrary contract

s. 69(1): a mortgagee may sell without the court only in the listed cases: certain English mortgages; where the deed expressly confers the power and the mortgagee is the Government; or where the deed expressly confers it and the property is in Kolkata, Chennai, Mumbai or a town the State notifies. Otherwise lenders use SARFAESI or a suit

s. 69(2): even where the power exists, it can be used only after a written notice demanding the principal has gone unpaid for three months, or interest of at least Rs 500 has been in arrear for three months
s. 69A: a mortgagee with a s. 69 power of sale may appoint a receiver of the income of the property; commission is capped at 5% of gross receipts unless the court allows otherwise

s. 65A: a mortgagor in lawful possession may grant leases binding on the mortgagee only on the terms in s. 65A(2) (ordinary management, best rent, no premium, buildings up to three years), unless the deed provides otherwise

s. 130-132: for unsecured receivables, take a signed written assignment and give each debtor express written notice, so that later payments to the assignor do not bind you; secured loans move with the security under the TPA and the Registration and Stamp Acts
consequences_stated: s. 59 with Registration Act s. 49: an unregistered mortgage deed that needed registration does not affect the property
s. 91-92: a surety or later encumbrancer who redeems is subrogated to the mortgagee's rights

instruments.short_name: Indian Trusts Act: trusts used in lending structures
instruments.title: Indian Trusts Act, 1882: creation of trusts, duties of trustees and breach of trust
instruments.theme: Mortgages, property and goods as security
applies_to: Lenders and arrangers using private trusts: securitisation trusts, security trustees for consortium loans and escrow or trust-and-retention accounts
Trustees holding security for lenders
key_concepts: Trust: an obligation annexed to ownership of property, arising from a confidence reposed in and accepted by the owner, for the benefit of another (s. 3)
The author of the trust, the trustee and the beneficiary; the subject is trust-property; a breach of trust is a breach of any duty imposed on a trustee as such (s. 3)
A person has notice of a fact when he knows it, or would have known it but for wilful abstention from inquiry or gross negligence (s. 3)
core_obligations: Structure security-trustee and securitisation arrangements so that the trust instrument records the trust property, the beneficiaries and the trustee's powers of enforcement
Trusts of immovable property must be declared by a registered instrument, as the Act requires (s. 5)

instruments.short_name: Aircraft Objects Act 2025: Cape Town security interests
instruments.title: Protection of Interests in Aircraft Objects Act, 2025: gives the Cape Town Convention and Aircraft Protocol the force of law in India
instruments.theme: Mortgages, property and goods as security
instruments.status: Enacted: comes into force on the date the Central Government notifies
applies_to: Lenders and lessors financing aircraft, airframes, aircraft engines and helicopters
Indian airline borrowers and lessees
key_concepts: Gives effect in India to the Convention on International Interests in Mobile Equipment and its Aircraft Protocol (Cape Town, 16 November 2001)
SARFAESI does not apply to security over aircraft (SARFAESI s. 31(c)); this Act supplies the creditor remedies for aircraft objects
core_obligations: s. 6: Article XI of the Protocol (remedies on insolvency), as declared by India, applies where the debtor is in India, the international interest is registered under the Convention and the parties have not excluded it in writing
s. 7: Article XIII of the Protocol (irrevocable de-registration and export request authorisation) applies, subject to the Bharatiya Vayuyan Adhiniyam, 2024 and its rules
s. 8: the High Court with territorial jurisdiction is the relevant court under Article 53 of the Convention
consequences_stated: s. 9: the Act prevails over any inconsistent law, but does not affect the Government's or public service providers' right to detain an aircraft for dues relating to services to that aircraft

instruments.short_name: SARFAESI Act: enforcing security without court
instruments.title: Securitisation and Reconstruction of Financial Assets and Enforcement of Security Interest Act, 2002
applies_to: Secured creditors as defined in the Act: banks, financial institutions, including NBFCs and HFCs only where they fall within a Central Government notification and meet its conditions, asset reconstruction companies and debenture trustees
Borrowers and guarantors whose secured assets are enforced
Every creditor filing security interests with CERSAI (Central Registry)
key_concepts: Enforcement without court: a security interest may be enforced by the secured creditor without the intervention of a court or tribunal, notwithstanding ss. 69-69A of the Transfer of Property Act (s. 13(1))
Central Registry (CERSAI) records creation, modification and satisfaction of security interests (Chapter IV)
Priority: once registered, the secured creditor's debts are paid in priority over all other debts and Government dues, subject to the IBC where insolvency proceedings are pending (s. 26E)

Exclusions: the Act does not apply to liens under the Contract or Sale of Goods Acts, pledges of movables, aircraft and vessels, unpaid sellers' rights, property not liable to attachment or sale under the first proviso to CPC s. 60(1) (but not property specifically charged with the debt), financial assets of Rs 1 lakh or less, agricultural land, or where the amount due is less than 20% of principal and interest (s. 31)
core_obligations: s. 13(2): after default and NPA classification, serve a written demand on the borrower to discharge the liability in full within 60 days; NPA classification is not needed for issuers of debt securities, where the debenture trustee enforces
s. 13(3): the notice must state the amount payable and the secured assets to be enforced
s. 13(3A): consider any representation or objection and, if rejecting it, communicate reasons within 15 days of receipt
s. 13(4): on non-payment, take possession of secured assets, take over management of the business, appoint a manager, or require third-party debtors to pay
s. 13(8): if the full dues and costs are tendered before publication of the auction or sale notice, the assets cannot be sold and the creditor must take no further step
s. 14: to take physical possession, apply to the Chief Metropolitan Magistrate or District Magistrate with the affidavit the proviso requires
s. 26D: no secured creditor may exercise Chapter III enforcement rights unless its security interest is registered with the Central Registry

s. 13(9): where more than one secured creditor finances the asset, s. 13(4) measures need the agreement of secured creditors holding at least 60% in value of the outstanding amount on a record date, subject to the IBC
s. 36: no s. 13(4) measure may be taken unless the claim is within the limitation period under the Limitation Act
timelines: 15 days: reply to the borrower's objection (s. 13(3A))
45 days: borrower's or aggrieved person's application to the DRT from the date of the measure (s. 17(1))
60 days: DRT to dispose of the s. 17 application, as far as possible (s. 17(5))
30 days: appeal by any aggrieved person to the DRAT (s. 18(1)); a borrower appealing must deposit 50% of the debt, reducible to 25%
consequences_stated: s. 18: no appeal to the DRAT is entertained unless the borrower deposits 50% of the debt claimed or determined, whichever is less; the DRAT may reduce it to not less than 25%
s. 26D: an unregistered security interest cannot be enforced under the Act

instruments.short_name: RDB Act: Debts Recovery Tribunals
instruments.title: Recovery of Debts and Bankruptcy Act, 1993 (formerly the Recovery of Debts Due to Banks and Financial Institutions Act)
applies_to: Banks, notified financial institutions, asset reconstruction companies and debenture trustees for secured debt securities
Borrowers and guarantors sued for debts of Rs 10 lakh or more (or other notified amount, not below Rs 1 lakh)
key_concepts: Threshold: the Act does not apply where the debt due is less than Rs 10 lakh or such other amount, not less than Rs 1 lakh, as the Central Government notifies (s. 1(4))

Financial institution: a public financial institution, a registered asset reconstruction company, a registered debenture trustee for secured debt securities, or any institution the Central Government notifies (s. 2(h))

Recovery certificate: the DRT issues a certificate and the Recovery Officer recovers by attachment and sale, taking possession of secured or other property, arrest and detention, or appointing a receiver (s. 25)
Priority: secured creditors' debts have priority over other debts and Government dues (s. 31B)
core_obligations: s. 19: file the original application before the DRT with jurisdiction; the defendant must file a written statement within 30 days of service of summons
s. 19: the DRT is to dispose of the application within 180 days of filing, as far as possible
s. 21: an appeal by the debtor is not entertained unless 50% of the debt determined is deposited, reducible to 25%
timelines: 30 days: appeal to the DRAT from receipt of the DRT order (s. 20(3)), extendable for sufficient cause
6 months: DRAT to endeavour to dispose of the appeal (s. 20(6))
consequences_stated: s. 26: the defendant cannot dispute the correctness of the amount in the recovery certificate before the Recovery Officer

instruments.short_name: Tribunals Reforms Act 2026: DRT, DRAT and consumer commissions
instruments.title: Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026: s. 6 substitutes ss. 6A and 15A of the RDB Act; s. 12 substitutes s. 55(1A) of the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
applies_to: Debts Recovery Tribunals and Appellate Tribunals; National and State consumer commissions
key_concepts: Qualifications, terms and service conditions of the DRT Presiding Officer (RDB s. 6A) and the DRAT Chairperson (RDB s. 15A) are now governed by the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026
The same applies to members of consumer commissions through the new Consumer Protection Act s. 55(1A)
core_obligations: No change to lenders' filing or recovery procedure; the amendments concern tribunal appointments and service conditions

instruments.short_name: Limitation Act: time limits for recovery suits
instruments.title: Limitation Act, 1963: periods for suits on loans, guarantees, promissory notes and mortgages, and fresh periods on acknowledgement or part-payment
applies_to: Every lender suing to recover a loan or enforce a mortgage, and borrowers and guarantors raising limitation as a defence
key_concepts: Money lent: three years from when the loan is made (Article 19); money lent under an agreement payable on demand: three years from when the loan is made, unless a written agreement makes it payable at a future time (Article 21). Instalment loans, acceleration clauses and guarantees can start time running at different points, so check the article that fits the claim
Bills of exchange, promissory notes and bonds: three years, running from dates that depend on the instrument's payment terms (Articles 34-37)
Suit to enforce payment of money secured by a mortgage or charged on immovable property: twelve years from when the money sued for becomes due (Article 62)
Mortgagee's suit for foreclosure: thirty years from when the mortgage money becomes due (Article 63(a)); for possession of mortgaged property: twelve years (Article 63(b))
Execution of a decree: twelve years from when the decree becomes enforceable (Article 136)
core_obligations: s. 18: obtain written acknowledgements of liability signed by the borrower or guarantor before the period expires; each gives a fresh period from the date it is signed
s. 19: a part-payment of principal or interest made before expiry gives a fresh period, provided it is acknowledged in writing by the payer
consequences_stated: s. 3: a suit filed after the prescribed period must be dismissed, even if limitation is not pleaded

instruments.short_name: Specific Relief Act: specific performance and injunctions
instruments.title: Specific Relief Act, 1963 (as amended in 2018): specific performance, substituted performance and injunctions
applies_to: Lenders enforcing security documents, undertakings and agreements to create security
Borrowers seeking injunctions against enforcement
key_concepts: Specific performance of a contract shall be enforced by the court, subject only to ss. 11(2), 14 and 16 (s. 10, as substituted in 2018)
Substituted performance: the party who suffers a breach may have the contract performed by a third party or itself and recover the costs (s. 20)
No injunction may be granted that would impede or delay an infrastructure project (s. 41(ha))
core_obligations: s. 20(2): before substituted performance, give the party in breach at least 30 days' written notice to perform; after substituted performance, specific performance cannot also be claimed (s. 20(3))

instruments.short_name: NI Act: cheque bounce (s. 138)
instruments.title: Negotiable Instruments Act, 1881: promissory notes, bills and cheques, and the offence of cheque dishonour (Chapter XVII, ss. 138-148)
applies_to: Lenders holding post-dated or security cheques and promissory notes from borrowers or guarantors
Drawers of cheques, and directors and officers of company drawers (s. 141)
key_concepts: Offence: a cheque drawn on the drawer's account for discharge of a legally enforceable debt or liability, returned unpaid for insufficient funds or exceeding the arrangement, is an offence punishable with imprisonment up to two years, fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both (s. 138)

Conditions: the cheque is presented within six months of its date or within its validity, whichever is earlier; a written demand is made within 30 days of the bank's return memo; and the drawer fails to pay within 15 days of receiving the notice (s. 138 proviso)
Company drawers: every person in charge of and responsible for the company's business is liable, subject to the defences in s. 141
Presumption that the holder received the cheque for discharge of a debt or liability, unless the contrary is proved (s. 139)
core_obligations: s. 138(b): send the demand notice within 30 days of the return information
s. 142(1)(b): file the complaint within one month of the date the cause of action arises (end of the 15-day payment period); the court may condone delay for sufficient cause
s. 143A: the court may order the drawer to pay interim compensation up to 20% of the cheque amount, within 60 days
s. 148: in an appeal against conviction the appellate court may order deposit of at least 20% of the fine or compensation
consequences_stated: s. 138: imprisonment up to two years, fine up to twice the cheque amount, or both
s. 147: offences under the Act are compoundable

instruments.short_name: Indian Stamp Act: duty on loan and security documents
instruments.title: Indian Stamp Act, 1899: stamp duty on loan agreements, mortgages, pledges, hypothecations and guarantees, and the effect of under-stamping
instruments.status: In force (as amended, with State amendments)
applies_to: Every lender executing loan, security or guarantee documents in India
Borrowers and guarantors who execute them
key_concepts: Duty rates are in Schedule I; most States substitute their own rates for instruments such as mortgages and agreements relating to deposit of title-deeds, pawn or pledge, so the State where the document is executed or the property lies usually decides the duty

Schedule I articles relevant to lending: Article 6 (agreement relating to deposit of title-deeds, pawn or pledge), Article 40 (mortgage deed) and Article 57 (security bond or mortgage deed executed by a surety)
core_obligations: s. 17: instruments chargeable with duty and executed in India must be stamped before or at the time of execution
Check the State Act or State Schedule for the rate; pay the higher-State differential where a document executed in one State is brought into another
consequences_stated: s. 35: an instrument not duly stamped is not admissible in evidence and cannot be acted upon, registered or authenticated, unless the duty and a penalty (Rs 5 or ten times the deficient duty, whichever is more) are paid
s. 33: a public officer or court before whom an unstamped instrument is produced must impound it

instruments.short_name: Maharashtra Stamp Act: title-deed deposits and mortgages
instruments.title: Maharashtra Stamp Act (Bom. Act 60 of 1958), Schedule I: Article 6 (agreement relating to deposit of title deeds, pawn, pledge or hypothecation), Article 40 (mortgage deed) and Article 54 (security bond or mortgage deed)
applies_to: Lenders taking mortgages, title-deed deposits, pledges or hypothecations over property in Maharashtra or under documents executed there
key_concepts: Article 6(1), deposit of title deeds: 0.1% of the amount secured (minimum Rs 100) where the amount does not exceed Rs 5 lakh; otherwise 0.3% of the amount secured, capped at Rs 20 lakh, and at Rs 50 lakh for an instrument in favour of a consortium of banks
Article 6(2) covers pawn, pledge or hypothecation of movable property; Article 40 covers mortgage deeds; Article 54 covers security bonds or mortgage deeds executed by sureties
core_obligations: Stamp title-deed deposit memoranda, mortgage deeds and hypothecation agreements at the Schedule I rates before or at execution

instruments.short_name: Other State stamp schedules: Delhi, Uttar Pradesh, Tamil Nadu
instruments.title: State stamp schedules for loan and security documents: Delhi (Schedule I-A), Uttar Pradesh (Schedule I-B) and Tamil Nadu (amendments to Schedule I, 2023)
instruments.reference_no: State amendments to the Indian Stamp Act, 1899
applies_to: Lenders executing or holding loan and security documents in Delhi, Uttar Pradesh or Tamil Nadu
key_concepts: Delhi charges duty on listed instruments under its own Schedule I-A to the Indian Stamp Act
Uttar Pradesh charges duty under Schedule I-B
Tamil Nadu amends Schedule I of the Indian Stamp Act directly; its 2023 amending Act revised rates for several instruments
core_obligations: Use the State schedule that applies to the instrument, not the central Schedule I rate, where the State has substituted its own

instruments.short_name: Registration Act: which loan documents must be registered
instruments.title: Registration Act, 1908: compulsory registration of documents affecting immovable property, time for presentation and the effect of non-registration
instruments.status: In force (as amended, with State amendments)
applies_to: Lenders taking registered mortgages, releases or assignments of rights in immovable property
Borrowers executing those documents
key_concepts: Compulsory registration: non-testamentary instruments that create, declare, assign, limit or extinguish any right, title or interest of Rs 100 or more in immovable property, and instruments acknowledging consideration for them (s. 17(1)(b)-(c))
A mortgage by deposit of title-deeds is not itself a registrable instrument; a document that records the terms of the mortgage may need registration depending on its contents

State amendments: some States, for example Gujarat, require a mortgagor who mortgages by deposit of title-deeds to file a notice with the registering officer within 30 days (State s. 89B), with penalties for failure (s. 89C)
core_obligations: s. 23: present documents for registration within four months of execution
Release or satisfaction deeds for registered mortgages should also be registered, as they extinguish an interest in immovable property
consequences_stated: s. 49: a document that must be registered but is not does not affect the property and is not evidence of the transaction, though it may be used as evidence of a contract in a suit for specific performance or of a collateral transaction

instruments.short_name: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam: electronic records as evidence
instruments.title: Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023: admissibility of electronic and digital records (ss. 61-63)
applies_to: Lenders relying on e-signed loan agreements, digital KYC, emails, app logs and system statements in court or tribunal proceedings
key_concepts: An electronic or digital record has the same legal effect, validity and enforceability as any other document, subject to s. 63 (s. 61)

A computer output is deemed a document and admissible without the original if the conditions in s. 63(2) are met: regular use of the device, regular feeding of information, proper operation and faithful reproduction (s. 63(1)-(2))
core_obligations: s. 63(4): file a certificate in the form in the Schedule with each electronic record tendered in evidence, signed by the person in charge of the device and an expert

instruments.short_name: Bankers' Books Evidence Act 2026: certified copies of bank records
instruments.title: Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 2026: proof of entries in bankers' books, including electronic, offsite and cloud records
applies_to: Banks and any entity or class of entities in the financial sector to whose books the Central Government extends the Act by notification (ss. 2(1)(a), 4)
Post office savings banks and money order offices
key_concepts: Bankers' books include ledgers, day-books, cash-books and all other records used in the ordinary course of business, whether physical or electronic, onsite, offsite, virtual or cloud, including back-up and disaster recovery sites (s. 2(1)(b))
A certified copy of an entry is prima facie evidence of the entry and admissible as evidence of the matters recorded, to the same extent as the original (s. 5)
An electronic or digital record of a banker's book is not to be denied admissibility because it is electronic, subject to the conditions in s. 7 (s. 6)
core_obligations: s. 3: certify copies with the certificate in the Schedules, dated and signed manually or by digital or electronic signature by the branch head, office head or an authorised officer, giving name and designation
s. 8: bank officers cannot be compelled to produce books or appear as witnesses in proceedings to which the bank is not a party, except by court order for special cause recorded in writing

instruments.short_name: Consumer Protection Act: lending as a 'service'
instruments.title: Consumer Protection Act, 2019: banking and financing as services, deficiency in service, unfair trade practices and consumer commissions
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Banks, NBFCs, HFCs and other lenders, as providers of a service
Borrowers and other consumers of financial services
key_concepts: 'Service' includes facilities in connection with banking and financing (s. 2(42))
Deficiency: any fault, imperfection, shortcoming or inadequacy in the quality, nature and manner of performance of a service (s. 2(11))
Unfair trade practice includes false or misleading representations to promote a service (s. 2(47))

Jurisdiction of the District, State and National Commissions turns on the consideration paid; the Act sets Rs 1 crore for District Commissions but lets the Central Government prescribe other limits, which it has done by rules, so check the current jurisdiction rules (s. 34(1))
core_obligations: Expect complaints about loan servicing, charges, disclosure and recovery conduct to be heard by consumer commissions in addition to RBI's grievance routes
timelines: 2 years: complaint to be filed within two years of the cause of action, unless delay is condoned (s. 69)

instruments.short_name: Tamil Nadu coercive-recovery law (2025)
instruments.title: Tamil Nadu Money Lending Entities (Prevention of Coercive Actions) Act, 2025, with the 2025 Rules and notifications under ss. 4 and 31
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: All money lending entities in Tamil Nadu (microfinance institutions, money lending agencies, firms, persons and digital lending platforms), except banks, RBI-registered NBFCs, co-operative banks and co-operative societies (s. 2)
RBI-registered NBFCs, co-operative banks and co-operative societies for the coercive-action provisions only (s. 2 proviso)
key_concepts: Micro loan: a loan to a household with annual income up to Rs 3 lakh, or a notified limit (s. 3(g))

Coercive action includes: violence, insult or intimidation; persistently following the borrower or family or interfering with their property; frequenting their home or workplace; using private or outsourced agencies to press for payment by coercion or undue influence; and forcibly taking government-benefit or other vital documents or household articles (s. 20(2))
District Collectors are the Registering Authorities (notification under s. 4(1), 16-02-2026)
core_obligations: Entities fully covered (not banks, RBI-registered NBFCs or co-operatives): s. 5: obtain a Certificate of Registration before granting or recovering any loan; the period for entities already operating was extended from 90 to 270 days from 19-11-2025 by the Removal of Difficulties Order of 04-08-2026

Entities fully covered: s. 9: display the effective interest rate; price loans with only four components (interest, processing charge, insurance premium and delayed penal payment); give a statement of terms one day before the loan, a standard loan agreement, a loan card and signed receipts; communicate in Tamil
Entities fully covered: s. 11: do not take security for loans up to the prescribed amount
All lenders in the State except banks, including RBI-registered NBFCs, co-operative banks and co-operative societies: s. 20: no coercive action against the borrower or family while recovering a loan
consequences_stated: s. 18: lending without registration, imprisonment up to three years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh
s. 21: coercive action, imprisonment up to three years or fine up to Rs 5 lakh, or both (clauses (a)-(c)); up to five years or fine up to Rs 5 lakh, or both (clauses (d)-(e))
s. 22: where a borrower or family member dies by suicide and coercive action immediately before it is proved, the lender is deemed to have abetted the suicide

instruments.short_name: Karnataka Money Lenders (Amendment) 2025: coercive recovery
instruments.title: Karnataka Money Lenders (Amendment) Act, 2025: shorter licences, ombudsperson, higher penalties and a ban on coercive recovery (s. 38A)
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Money lenders licensed or unlicensed under the Karnataka Money Lenders Act, 1961
Borrowers in Karnataka
key_concepts: Licence period cut from five years to three years (s. 10, as amended)
Officers of listed State departments must report contraventions of the Act and of the Karnataka Prohibition of Charging Exorbitant Interest Act, 2004 (s. 15(4))
Ombudsperson to mediate disputes and a grievance redressal forum (new ss. 15A-15B)
No person may charge exorbitant interest, and money lenders may not use coercive action, themselves or through agents or family, to recover money (new s. 38A)
core_obligations: s. 38A: no coercive recovery; coercive recovery is punishable and may lead to suspension or cancellation of the money lender's registration
consequences_stated: s. 37(2) and s. 38: maximum imprisonment raised to ten years and maximum fine to Rs 5 lakh

instruments.short_name: Assam microfinance money-lending law (2020)
instruments.title: Assam Micro Finance Institutions (Regulation of Money Lending) Act, 2020
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Micro finance institutions and money lending agencies or organisations in Assam, including companies, NBFCs as defined in the Act and societies, whose principal or incidental activity is lending to poor or below-poverty-line borrowers
key_concepts: Aims to protect economically vulnerable borrowers from usurious interest rates and coercive recovery by microfinance institutions and money lending agencies (Preamble)
Borrower includes individuals, self-help groups and joint liability groups borrowing for a productive purpose
core_obligations: Registration with the State authority before lending, with renewal, and powers to suspend or cancel registration

instruments.short_name: Tamil Nadu Money-lenders Act 1957
instruments.title: Tamil Nadu Money-lenders Act, 1957: licensing of money-lenders, permitted interest and charges, accounts and receipts, and penalties for molesting debtors
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Money-lenders carrying on business in Tamil Nadu, as defined in the Act
key_concepts: Money-lenders must obtain a licence (s. 3), exhibit their names (s. 6) and charge only the interest and charges allowed (s. 7)
Molestation of a debtor is an offence (s. 14); the court may limit interest recoverable and allow instalments (ss. 20-A, 20-B)
core_obligations: s. 9: keep books and give receipts and statements of account to debtors

instruments.short_name: Payment and Settlement Systems Act: e-mandate bounce (s. 25)
instruments.title: Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007: authorisation of payment systems and the offence of dishonour of an electronic funds transfer
instruments.theme: Payments, credit information and anti-money laundering
applies_to: Lenders collecting EMIs through ECS, NACH or other electronic mandates
Payment system operators and banks
key_concepts: No person other than RBI may commence or operate a payment system without RBI authorisation (s. 4)
Dishonour of an electronic funds transfer for insufficient funds is an offence on the same pattern as NI Act s. 138: imprisonment up to two years, fine up to twice the amount, or both (s. 25(1))
Banks and system providers may not charge a person for paying or receiving by the electronic modes the law specifies (s. 10A)
core_obligations: s. 25(1)(c)-(d): to prosecute an e-mandate dishonour, send a written demand within 30 days of the bank's information about the dishonour; the offence is complete if the payer fails to pay within 15 days of the notice
s. 25(1)(b): the transfer must have been initiated in accordance with the system provider's procedural guidelines
consequences_stated: s. 25: imprisonment up to two years, fine up to twice the transfer amount, or both

instruments.short_name: PSS Act s. 10A amended (2026)
instruments.title: Taxation and Other Laws (Amendment) Act, 2026, s. 2: amendment of s. 10A of the Payment and Settlement Systems Act, 2007
instruments.theme: Payments, credit information and anti-money laundering
applies_to: Banks and payment system providers
key_concepts: The no-charge rule in PSS s. 10A now covers the electronic modes of payment notified by the Central Government, instead of the modes prescribed under s. 269SU of the Income-tax Act, 1961
core_obligations: Check fee schedules against the Central Government's notified list of electronic payment modes

instruments.short_name: Credit Information Companies Act: bureau reporting and corrections
instruments.title: Credit Information Companies (Regulation) Act, 2005: membership of credit bureaus, reporting, accuracy, borrower access and corrections
instruments.theme: Payments, credit information and anti-money laundering
applies_to: Credit institutions (banks, NBFCs, HFCs and others notified), credit information companies and specified users
Borrowers whose credit information is reported
key_concepts: Every credit institution must be a member of at least one credit information company (s. 15)
Credit information may be disclosed only to specified users and only for permitted purposes (s. 17(4))
Credit institutions, bureaus and specified users must keep credit information accurate, complete and protected against loss or unauthorised access (s. 19)
core_obligations: s. 17(2): furnish credit information to the bureau within the period in its notice
s. 21(1)-(2): on request, give a loan applicant a copy of the credit information obtained, for the charge set by RBI regulations

s. 21(3): update or correct a borrower's information within 30 days of a request; bureaus correct only on the credit institution's certification, and not while a dispute is pending before a court, tribunal or arbitrator
consequences_stated: s. 22: unauthorised access to credit information, fine up to Rs 1 lakh per offence and Rs 10,000 a day for continuing access
s. 23: fines up to Rs 1 crore for listed contraventions, including failure to furnish information or making false statements

instruments.short_name: Credit Information Companies Rules 2006
instruments.title: Credit Information Companies Rules, 2006 (Department of Financial Services)
instruments.issuing_department: Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services
instruments.theme: Payments, credit information and anti-money laundering
applies_to: Credit institutions, credit information companies and specified users
key_concepts: Rules under CICRA on appeals to the appellate authority, security safeguards, collection and accuracy of data, disclosure of disputed data, updating of credit information and fidelity and secrecy
core_obligations: Follow the security safeguards and data-accuracy procedures in the rules when collecting, storing, correcting and sharing credit information

instruments.short_name: Credit Information Companies Regulations 2006
instruments.title: Credit Information Companies Regulations, 2006 (Reserve Bank of India)
instruments.theme: Payments, credit information and anti-money laundering
applies_to: Credit institutions, credit information companies and specified users
key_concepts: RBI regulations under CICRA on registration of credit information companies (Forms A and B), the notice for collecting credit information (Form C), privacy principles, personal data and the charges a credit information company may levy
core_obligations: Furnish and correct credit information in the form and within the periods the regulations and the bureau's notice set

instruments.short_name: Registration of Assignment of Receivables Rules 2012
instruments.title: Registration of Assignment of Receivables Rules, 2012 under the Factoring Regulation Act, 2011 (filing with the Central Registry)
instruments.issuing_department: Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services
instruments.theme: Mortgages, property and goods as security
applies_to: Factors and other assignees of receivables
key_concepts: Particulars of every assignment of receivables in favour of a factor are filed with the Central Register kept under SARFAESI s. 22 (CERSAI)
core_obligations: File particulars of each assignment of receivables with the Central Registry in the prescribed form and fee

instruments.short_name: Draft Registration Bill 2025 (would replace the 1908 Act)
instruments.title: Registration Bill, 2025 (draft published by the Department of Land Resources for comments)
instruments.issuing_department: Ministry of Rural Development, Department of Land Resources
instruments.status: Proposed: draft published for comments; not introduced in Parliament
applies_to: Lenders taking mortgages by deposit of title-deeds and other security over immovable property
Property owners and borrowers
key_concepts: Would repeal and replace the Registration Act, 1908
Online registration: electronic presentation and admission, electronic certificates and digital records; Aadhaar-based authentication with consent, with alternatives
Wider compulsory registration: agreements to sell, powers of attorney to transfer property, sale certificates and documents setting out the terms of a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds

Banks, financial institutions and other creditors lending on a mortgage by deposit of title-deeds must file a copy of the title deed with the registering officer and notify the mortgage; a filed mortgage would take effect against any unfiled one over the same property
core_obligations: No obligation until enacted; lenders' title-deed mortgage processes would need a filing step if it passes in this form

instruments.short_name: Private Member's Bill: Consumer Protection (Amendment) 2025
instruments.title: Consumer Protection (Amendment) Bill, 2025 (Private Member's Bill No. 39 of 2025, Lok Sabha)
instruments.status: Proposed: Private Member's Bill pending in the Lok Sabha
applies_to: Consumers and service providers under the Consumer Protection Act, 2019
key_concepts: Introduced by a private member; Private Members' Bills rarely become law

instruments.short_name: Private Member's Bill: Information Technology (Amendment) 2025
instruments.title: Information Technology (Amendment) Bill, 2025 (Private Member's Bill No. 28 of 2025, Lok Sabha)
instruments.status: Proposed: Private Member's Bill pending in the Lok Sabha
applies_to: Intermediaries and others under the Information Technology Act, 2000
key_concepts: Introduced by a private member; Private Members' Bills rarely become law

instruments.short_name: Private Member's Bill: Prevention of Money-laundering (Amendment) 2025
instruments.title: Prevention of Money-laundering (Amendment) Bill, 2025 (Private Member's Bill No. 75 of 2025, Lok Sabha)
instruments.status: Proposed: Private Member's Bill pending in the Lok Sabha
applies_to: Reporting entities under the PMLA
key_concepts: Introduced by a private member; Private Members' Bills rarely become law

instruments.short_name: Repealing and Amending Act 2025: notices by speed post
instruments.title: Repealing and Amending Act, 2025: repeal of spent amending Acts and replacement of 'registered post' with 'speed post with registration' in the General Clauses Act and the CPC
applies_to: Every lender serving statutory notices by post, including SARFAESI and NI Act demand notices
key_concepts: General Clauses Act, 1897 s. 27: service by post is now deemed effected by properly addressing, pre-paying and posting by 'speed post with registration' instead of 'registered post'
Corresponding changes to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908
Repeals spent amending Acts, including the Arbitration amendments of 2015 and 2021, the NI amendment of 2018 and the Factoring amendment of 2021; the changes they made to the principal Acts remain
core_obligations: Update notice templates and dispatch processes to use speed post with registration where a law requires service by post

instruments.short_name: Board for Payment and Settlement Systems Regulations 2008 (superseded)
instruments.title: Board for Regulation and Supervision of Payment and Settlement Systems Regulations, 2008
instruments.status: Superseded by the Payments Regulatory Board Regulations, 2025
applies_to: RBI's payment systems oversight board (historical)
key_concepts: Replaced by the Payments Regulatory Board constituted under the amended PSS Act and its 2025 regulations (20-05-2025)

instruments.short_name: PMLA: records, reporting and enhanced due diligence
instruments.title: Prevention of Money-laundering Act, 2002: obligations of reporting entities (Chapter IV, ss. 11A-15)
instruments.theme: Payments, credit information and anti-money laundering
applies_to: Reporting entities: banking companies, financial institutions (which include NBFCs, housing finance institutions, chit fund companies and payment system operators), intermediaries and persons carrying on designated businesses (ss. 2(1)(l), 2(1)(wa))
Designated directors and employees of reporting entities
key_concepts: Financial institution includes a non-banking financial company, a housing finance institution, a chit fund company and a payment system operator (s. 2(1)(l))
Offence of money-laundering: rigorous imprisonment of three to seven years and fine (s. 4)
core_obligations: s. 12(1)(a)-(b): keep a record of all transactions that allows each to be reconstructed, and report prescribed transactions, attempted or executed, to the Director (FIU-IND) within the prescribed time
s. 12(1)(e): keep records of documents evidencing the identity of clients and beneficial owners, account files and business correspondence
s. 12(2): keep all such information confidential
s. 12(3)-(4): keep transaction records for five years from the transaction, and identity records for five years after the relationship ends or the account is closed, whichever is later

s. 12AA: before each specified transaction, verify the client's identity by Aadhaar authentication (or another prescribed mode), examine ownership, financial position and sources of funds, and record the purpose; do not allow the transaction if the client fails these steps
consequences_stated: s. 13(2): the Director may warn, direct compliance or reporting, or impose a penalty of Rs 10,000 to Rs 1 lakh for each failure on the reporting entity, its designated director or employees

instruments.short_name: Chit Funds Act: chit business by companies
instruments.title: Chit Funds Act, 1982: sanction and registration of chits, and limits on chit fund companies
applies_to: Foremen and companies conducting chits
Groups and lenders that might run chit or chit-like schemes
key_concepts: The Act is administered by the State Governments through their Registrars of Chits
A chit fund company is a 'financial institution' and a reporting entity under the PMLA (PMLA s. 2(1)(l))
core_obligations: s. 4: no chit may be commenced or conducted without the previous sanction of the State Government and registration of the chit
s. 12: a company carrying on chit business may not conduct any other business without the general or special permission of the State Government
s. 13: the aggregate chit amount a foreman may conduct is capped, for a company by reference to a multiple of its net owned funds

instruments.short_name: Maharashtra depositors' protection law (MPID Act)
instruments.title: Maharashtra Protection of Interest of Depositors (in Financial Establishments) Act, 1999
applies_to: Any person accepting deposits in Maharashtra under any scheme or arrangement, other than banking companies and corporations or co-operative societies owned or controlled by the Government (s. 2(d))
key_concepts: Deposit excludes, among others, share capital and SEBI-regulated debentures and bonds, partners' capital, amounts from banks and specified financial institutions, ordinary-course security deposits and advances, and chit subscriptions (s. 2(c))
Financial establishments are not limited to unregistered entities: any deposit-taking person outside the s. 2(d) exclusions is covered
core_obligations: Repay deposits on maturity with the promised returns; the State may attach the money and property of a defaulting establishment (s. 4)
consequences_stated: s. 3: on fraudulent default in repaying deposits, every promoter, partner, director, manager or employee responsible for the business is punishable with imprisonment up to six years and fine

instruments.short_name: Maharashtra Money-Lending (Regulation) Act 2014
instruments.title: Maharashtra Money-Lending (Regulation) Act, 2014
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Money-lenders in Maharashtra: individuals, Hindu undivided families, companies other than RBI-regulated NBFCs, and unincorporated bodies, including pawn-brokers (s. 2(14))
excluded: Banks, co-operative banks, multi-State co-operative banks and non-banking financial companies are excluded from 'money-lender' (s. 2(14))
Loans to or by a bank, insurance company, co-operative society or Government are not 'loans' under the Act (s. 2(13))
key_concepts: The Act licenses and regulates private money-lenders; RBI-regulated lenders are outside it
core_obligations: Money-lenders covered by the Act must be licensed and follow its rules on interest, accounts and recovery

instruments.short_name: Karnataka Money Lenders Act 1961
instruments.title: Karnataka Money Lenders Act, 1961 (principal Act; see the 2025 amendment for the coercive-recovery ban)
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Money lenders carrying on business in Karnataka, as defined in the Act
key_concepts: Banks, as defined in s. 2(1), are outside the definition of money lender
The 2025 amendment shortened licences to three years, added an ombudsperson and banned coercive recovery (new s. 38A)
core_obligations: Money lenders covered by the Act must be licensed and keep accounts as it requires

instruments.short_name: Arbitration and Conciliation Act: loan arbitration
instruments.title: Arbitration and Conciliation Act, 1996: arbitration agreements, interim relief, appointment and independence of arbitrators, time limits, setting aside and enforcement of awards
applies_to: Lenders whose loan or security documents contain an arbitration clause
Borrowers and guarantors bound by such clauses
key_concepts: An arbitration agreement must be in writing; it may be a clause in a contract or a separate agreement, and an exchange of communications by electronic means that records the agreement counts (s. 7)

Interim measures from the court before or during the arbitration, or after the award but before enforcement, including securing the amount in dispute and the preservation, custody or sale of goods (s. 9(1)); interim measures from the arbitral tribunal, enforceable as if they were court orders (s. 17)

Independence of arbitrators: a prospective arbitrator must disclose circumstances giving rise to justifiable doubts about independence or impartiality (s. 12(1)); a person whose relationship with the parties, counsel or the dispute falls in the Seventh Schedule is ineligible, notwithstanding any prior agreement, unless the parties waive this by an express written agreement after the dispute has arisen (s. 12(5))
Once the arbitral tribunal is constituted, the court will not entertain a s. 9 application unless the remedy under s. 17 may not be efficacious (s. 9(3))
The Limitation Act, 1963 applies to arbitrations as it applies to court proceedings (s. 43)
core_obligations: s. 9(2): where the court grants an interim measure before the arbitration starts, commence the arbitral proceedings within 90 days of the order, or within any further time the court allows

s. 29A(1): in domestic arbitrations the award must be made within twelve months from completion of pleadings; the parties may extend by consent for up to six months (s. 29A(3)), after which only the court can extend the mandate (s. 29A(4))
s. 34(3): an application to set aside an award must be made within three months of receiving it, with a further 30 days only on sufficient cause

s. 36: once the time to challenge has expired the award is enforced like a court decree under the CPC; filing a s. 34 challenge does not by itself stay the award, and a stay of a money award is considered with regard to the CPC rules on stay of money decrees; where the court is satisfied that there is a prima facie case that the arbitration agreement, the underlying contract or the making of the award was induced by fraud or corruption, it stays the award unconditionally pending the s. 34 challenge (s. 36(3), second proviso)
consequences_stated: s. 29A(4): if the award is not made in time and the court does not extend the period, the arbitrator's mandate terminates; the court may cut the arbitrator's fees by up to 5% for each month of delay attributable to the tribunal
s. 12(5): an arbitrator who is ineligible under the Seventh Schedule cannot act unless the parties have expressly waived it in writing after the dispute arose

instruments.short_name: Factoring Regulation Act: assignment of receivables
instruments.title: Factoring Regulation Act, 2011: registration of factors with RBI, assignment of receivables, notice to debtors and filing with the Central Registry
instruments.theme: Mortgages, property and goods as security
applies_to: Factors: RBI-registered NBFCs, banks, statutory corporations and companies engaged in the factoring business (s. 2(i))
Assignors (sellers of goods and services) and debtors whose receivables are assigned
key_concepts: Factoring business: acquiring receivables by assignment for consideration, for collection or for financing against the assignment; credit facilities provided by a bank or an NBFC in its ordinary course of business against security of receivables are excluded (s. 2(j)(i))

No factor may commence or carry on factoring business without a certificate of registration from RBI; the NBFC registration requirements of the RBI Act apply (s. 3). Banks, corporations set up under a Central or State Act and Government companies do not need this registration (s. 5)
An assignment of receivables must be by agreement in writing, and the assignor must disclose the debtor's defences and rights of set-off to the assignee (s. 7)

The assignee cannot demand payment from the debtor until notice of the assignment is given to the debtor (s. 8); once notice is given the debtor must pay the assignee, and payment to the assignee in discharge of the receivables specified in the notice fully discharges the debtor to that extent (s. 9)
Recovery of an assigned receivable through a court or tribunal must be within the period of limitation under the Limitation Act (s. 28)
core_obligations: s. 19(1): register the particulars of every assignment of receivables in the factor's favour with the Central Registry set up under SARFAESI, within the time and in the manner prescribed; where receivables are financed through a Trade Receivables Discounting System, the TReDS files on the factor's behalf (s. 19(1A))
consequences_stated: s. 21: default in filing under s. 19 makes the company and every officer in default liable to a penalty of up to Rs 5 lakh, and up to Rs 10,000 a day while it continues, imposed by RBI
s. 22: failure to comply with an RBI direction, penalty of up to Rs 5 lakh, and up to Rs 10,000 a day while it continues
s. 23: contraventions with no specific penalty, imprisonment up to one year, fine, or both; courts take cognizance only on a complaint by an authorised RBI officer (s. 24)

instruments.short_name: Information Technology Act: e-contracts, e-signatures, data security
instruments.title: Information Technology Act, 2000: legal recognition of electronic records and signatures, electronic contracts, and data-security liabilities
applies_to: Lenders and digital lenders executing loan documents electronically or using e-signatures and Aadhaar e-KYC based e-sign
Bodies corporate handling sensitive personal data
key_concepts: Where a law requires a signature, an electronic signature in the prescribed manner satisfies it (s. 5); electronic signature techniques include Aadhaar or other e-KYC based e-authentication (s. 3A and Second Schedule)
A contract is not unenforceable merely because the proposal, acceptance or revocation was expressed in electronic form (s. 10A)

The Act does not apply to the documents in the First Schedule (s. 1(4)). Since 26-09-2022 the exclusion for negotiable instruments does not cover a cheque, demand promissory note or bill of exchange issued in favour of or endorsed by an entity regulated by RBI, NHB, SEBI, IRDAI or PFRDA, and the exclusion for powers of attorney does not cover one that empowers such a regulated entity to act for the executant; trusts and wills remain excluded. The same 2022 notification (S.O. 4720(E)) omitted the entry for contracts for the sale or conveyance of immovable property; stamp duty and registration law still apply to such contracts
core_obligations: s. 43A: a body corporate handling sensitive personal data must implement and maintain reasonable security practices; s. 43A is omitted from 13-05-2027 by the Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (see the DPDP section)
s. 72A: do not disclose personal information obtained under a lawful contract without the person's consent, with intent to cause or knowing it likely to cause wrongful loss or gain
consequences_stated: s. 43A: negligence in maintaining reasonable security practices that causes wrongful loss or gain makes the body corporate liable to pay damages by way of compensation
s. 66C: fraudulent or dishonest use of another person's electronic signature, password or other unique identification feature, imprisonment up to three years and fine up to Rs 1 lakh

instruments.short_name: BUDS Act: ban on unregulated deposit schemes
instruments.title: Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Act, 2019: ban on unregulated deposit schemes, fraudulent default in regulated schemes, and information to the central database
applies_to: Deposit takers: individuals, firms, LLPs, companies, associations, trusts, co-operative societies and any other arrangement receiving or soliciting deposits (s. 2(6))
Promoters and persons inducing investment in unregulated schemes
excluded: Statutory corporations, banking companies, SBI, regional rural banks and co-operative banks are not deposit takers (s. 2(6))

Loans received from banks, public financial institutions, RBI-registered NBFCs, regional financial institutions and insurers, Government and statutory authorities, and partners' capital, are not deposits (s. 2(4))
key_concepts: Deposit: money received as an advance, loan or in any other form with a promise to return it, with or without interest or other benefit, subject to the exclusions in s. 2(4)

Regulated Deposit Schemes are those listed in the First Schedule, including deposits accepted by RBI-registered NBFCs, and schemes regulated under the RBI Act or by SEBI, IRDAI and the State Governments; every other deposit scheme is an Unregulated Deposit Scheme and is banned (s. 3)
Prize chits and money circulation schemes banned under the 1978 Act are deemed Unregulated Deposit Schemes (s. 6)
core_obligations: s. 3: do not promote, operate, advertise or accept deposits under an Unregulated Deposit Scheme
s. 4: a deposit taker under a Regulated Deposit Scheme must not commit fraudulent default in repayment or in rendering a promised service

s. 10(1): a deposit taker must intimate the authority maintaining the central database about its business, in the prescribed form and time; this applies to companies accepting deposits under Chapter V of the Companies Act, 2013
consequences_stated: s. 21: soliciting deposits under a banned scheme, imprisonment of one to five years and fine of Rs 2 lakh to Rs 10 lakh; accepting them, two to seven years and Rs 3 lakh to Rs 10 lakh; accepting and fraudulently defaulting, three to ten years and fine of Rs 5 lakh up to twice the funds collected
s. 22: fraudulent default in a Regulated Deposit Scheme, imprisonment up to seven years, or fine of Rs 5 lakh up to Rs 25 crore or three times the profits made, whichever is higher, or both
s. 23: false or misleading inducement to invest in a banned scheme, imprisonment of one to five years and fine up to Rs 10 lakh

instruments.short_name: BUDS Rules 2020
instruments.title: Banning of Unregulated Deposit Schemes Rules, 2020
instruments.issuing_department: Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services
applies_to: Deposit takers required to intimate their business under s. 10 of the BUDS Act
key_concepts: Rules under the BUDS Act on the form, manner and time for deposit takers to give information about their business to the central database authority
core_obligations: File the intimation of deposit-taking business in the form and within the time the rules prescribe

instruments.short_name: Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules 2002
instruments.title: Security Interest (Enforcement) Rules, 2002 under the SARFAESI Act: demand notice, possession, valuation and sale of secured assets
instruments.issuing_department: Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services
applies_to: Secured creditors and their authorised officers enforcing security under SARFAESI s. 13
Borrowers and guarantors whose assets are sold
key_concepts: The authorised officer is an officer of the secured creditor designated by its Board to exercise the secured creditor's rights (rule 2)
Movable assets: possession, valuation and fixing of a reserve price, and sale by quotations, public tender, public auction or private treaty (rules 4 to 6)
Immovable assets: possession notice, valuation by an approved valuer and fixing of a reserve price before sale (rule 8)
core_obligations: Rules 6(2) and 8(6): serve the borrower a notice of thirty days for sale of the secured asset; for sale by public tender or auction, publish a public notice in two leading newspapers, one in the vernacular, setting out the terms of sale including the reserve price

Rule 9(1): no sale of immovable property before thirty days from the public notice of sale or service of the sale notice on the borrower; the rule was amended in 2016 to provide a shorter notice for a re-sale after a failed first sale

Rule 9(3)-(4): the purchaser pays a 25% deposit on the sale and the balance within the period the rule allows, which may be extended only within the limits the rule sets (these sub-rules were amended in 2016); a sale certificate issues on confirmation and payment (rule 9(6))
consequences_stated: Rule 9(5): if the purchaser defaults on the balance, the deposit is forfeited and the property is resold

instruments.short_name: CERSAI (Central Registry) Rules 2011
instruments.title: SARFAESI (Central Registry) Rules, 2011, as amended in 2013 and 2016: filing security interests and assignments with CERSAI
instruments.issuing_department: Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services
instruments.theme: Mortgages, property and goods as security
applies_to: Secured creditors registering the creation, modification and satisfaction of security interests
Factors and assignees filing assignments of receivables
key_concepts: Since the 2016 amendment, filings cover mortgages other than by deposit of title-deeds, hypothecation of plant and machinery, stocks, book debts and receivables, intangible assets such as know-how, patents, trade marks and licences, and under-construction buildings secured otherwise than by mortgage (rule 4(2A)-(2D))
Filings are made in the prescribed forms and authenticated with a valid digital signature (rule 4)
core_obligations: Rule 5(1): file the particulars of each transaction with the Central Registrar within thirty days of the transaction
Pay the filing fee in the Table under rule 7; delays up to a further thirty days may be condoned on application, with a higher fee
consequences_stated: SARFAESI s. 26D: a secured creditor cannot exercise its enforcement rights under Chapter III of SARFAESI unless the security interest is registered with the Central Registry

SARFAESI s. 26E: debts due to a secured creditor with a registered security interest get priority over other debts and government dues, subject to the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 where proceedings under that Code are pending

instruments.short_name: DRT (Procedure) Rules 1993
instruments.title: Debts Recovery Tribunal (Procedure) Rules, 1993: filing, fees, documents and hearing of recovery applications
instruments.issuing_department: Ministry of Finance, Department of Financial Services
instruments.reference_no: Rules under s. 36 of the RDB Act
applies_to: Banks and financial institutions filing recovery applications before a Debts Recovery Tribunal
Defendants (borrowers and guarantors)
key_concepts: Procedure for filing and scrutiny of applications (rules 4 and 5), place of filing (rule 6), application fees (rule 7), documents to accompany the application (rule 9) and the respondent's reply (rule 12)
The application form sets out the particulars of the applicant and defendant, jurisdiction, limitation, facts and the relief sought
core_obligations: Rule 11: endorse a copy of the application and documents to the respondent
Rule 7: pay the application fee in the scale the rule sets

instruments.short_name: Karnataka micro loan coercive-recovery law (2025)
instruments.title: Karnataka Micro Loan and Small Loan (Prevention of Coercive Actions) Act, 2025 (replacing the Ordinance of 12-02-2025)
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Micro finance institutions, money lending agencies, organisations and lenders operating in Karnataka, including firms, persons, groups and digital lending platforms whose principal or incidental activity is lending at interest (s. 2(1)(e))
excluded: Banks (including small finance banks, local area banks, regional rural banks and their business correspondents) regulated by RBI, co-operative banks and societies, souharda societies, and NBFCs and housing finance companies registered with RBI (s. 1(3))
key_concepts: Lenders within the Act must register with the district Registering Authority (the Deputy Commissioner) before granting or recovering loans (s. 3(2)); registration is for one year and renewal is sought sixty days before expiry (s. 3(3)-(4))

Coercive action includes pressure, violence, insults or intimidation of the borrower or family, persistent following, frequenting the home or workplace, using outside agencies or persons with a criminal background, and forcibly taking documents for Government benefits (s. 8, Explanation)

If an unregistered lender resorts to coercive action against a borrower from a vulnerable section of society, loans made before the commencement are deemed discharged and civil suits for recovery are barred (s. 15)
core_obligations: s. 6: take no security by pawn, pledge or any collateral; security taken before the Act stands released

s. 7: price loans only through interest, processing charge, insurance premium and delayed penal payment; give a loan card in Kannada with the effective rate of interest; display the rate in offices, literature and website; give receipts and copies of documents
s. 7(11): file quarterly and annual statements with the Registering Authority before the 10th day of the following quarter or year
s. 8: no coercive action, directly or through agents, to recover a loan
consequences_stated: s. 13: coercive recovery, imprisonment up to ten years and fine up to Rs 5 lakh; offences are cognizable and non-bailable
s. 7(12): failure to file the quarterly or annual statement, imprisonment for six months, fine up to Rs 10,000, or both
s. 4: registration may be suspended or cancelled; a conviction under the Act is sufficient cause

instruments.short_name: Karnataka exorbitant-interest law (amended 2025)
instruments.title: Karnataka Prohibition of Charging Exorbitant Interest Act, 2004, as amended by Karnataka Act 17 of 2025
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
instruments.reference_no: Karnataka Act 14 of 2004, amended by Karnataka Act 17 of 2025
applies_to: Any person lending money in Karnataka, and money lenders under the Karnataka Money Lenders Act, 1961
key_concepts: Exorbitant interest is interest charged on an hourly, daily, instalment, monthly or other basis at a rate above the rate the State fixes under s. 28 of the Karnataka Money Lenders Act, 1961 (s. 2(1)(b))
The 2025 amendment added a ban on coercive recovery by money lenders, with the same list of coercive actions as the 2025 micro loan law (s. 3(2)), and powers to suspend or cancel registration (s. 4A)
core_obligations: s. 3(1): charge no exorbitant interest on any loan
s. 3(2): no coercive action, by the lender, its agents or family members, to recover money
consequences_stated: s. 4: contravention of s. 3 or molestation of a debtor, imprisonment up to ten years and fine up to Rs 5 lakh

s. 5: a debtor may deposit the amount due with interest at the State rate in court and seek an order recording satisfaction of the loan; the court may order restoration of property forcibly taken (s. 6)

instruments.short_name: Andhra Pradesh microfinance law (2011)
instruments.title: Andhra Pradesh Micro Finance Institutions (Regulation of Money Lending) Act, 2011
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Micro finance institutions lending to women self-help groups and their members in Andhra Pradesh, which by definition include companies and NBFCs whose principal or incidental activity is lending to the below poverty line population (s. 2(d))
key_concepts: MFIs must register with the district Registering Authority, stating the area of operation, interest rates, due-diligence and recovery systems (s. 3)
Interest recovered may not exceed the principal; a loan stands discharged once twice the principal has been realised (s. 9)
No further loan to an SHG with an outstanding bank loan without the Registering Authority's prior written approval, and no loan to an SHG member during two subsisting loans from any source (s. 10)

Challenges by microfinance NBFCs to the State's power to regulate them were disposed of by the High Court in 2013 without deciding legislative competence. The Supreme Court later held (for the Kerala and Gujarat money lenders Acts) that state money-lending laws do not apply to RBI-regulated NBFCs (Nedumpilli Finance Co. v. State of Kerala, 2022 INSC 545)
core_obligations: s. 8: display interest rates; charge nothing beyond the prescribed application charge

s. 11: give the borrower a loan statement within seven days with the effective rate of interest, signed receipts and copies of documents; repayments are made at the Gram Panchayat office or a designated public place; no recovery agents and no coercive recovery
s. 12: file a monthly statement of borrowers, loans and interest with the Registering Authority before the 10th of each month
consequences_stated: s. 16: persons responsible for an MFI who use coercive measures against SHGs, members or their families, imprisonment up to three years, fine up to Rs 1 lakh, or both
s. 17: carrying on business without registration, or lending in breach of s. 10, is separately punishable

instruments.short_name: Kerala Money Lenders Act 1958
instruments.title: Kerala Money Lenders Act, 1958
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Money lenders in Kerala: persons whose main or subsidiary occupation is advancing and realising loans, including branch and liaison offices and pawn brokers (s. 2(7))
excluded: Banks and co-operative societies, LIC and certain other named statutory institutions (s. 2(7))
NBFCs registered with and regulated by RBI: the Supreme Court held that the Act does not apply to them (Nedumpilli Finance Co. v. State of Kerala, 2022 INSC 545)
key_concepts: No person, firm, joint family or unincorporated association may carry on business as a money lender without a licence (s. 3)
Molestation includes obstructing, using violence to or intimidating the debtor, interfering with their property, or annoying or intimidating family members (s. 2(6))
core_obligations: s. 7(1): charge no interest above 18% a year plus a 2% processing charge, or any rate the Government notifies
s. 6: display the name and the words 'money lender' or 'pawn-broker' over the place of business
consequences_stated: s. 13: molesting a debtor to recover a loan, imprisonment up to six months, fine up to Rs 10,000, or both
s. 17: lending without a licence or in breach of its conditions, imprisonment of three months to three years and fine up to Rs 5 lakh

instruments.short_name: Kerala exorbitant-interest law (2012)
instruments.title: Kerala Prohibition of Charging Exorbitant Interest Act, 2012
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Any person lending money in Kerala
key_concepts: Exorbitant interest is interest above the rate under s. 7(1) of the Kerala Money Lenders Act, 1958, and includes daily, hourly, kandu and meter vatti and thandal (s. 2(1)(c))
Offences under the Act are cognizable and non-bailable (s. 4)
core_obligations: s. 3: charge no exorbitant interest on any loan
consequences_stated: s. 9(1): charging exorbitant interest, imprisonment up to three years and fine up to Rs 50,000; harassing a debtor mentally or physically to recover a loan, imprisonment up to one year and fine up to Rs 10,000
s. 5: a debtor may deposit the amount due in court and seek an order recording satisfaction of the loan

instruments.short_name: Tamil Nadu exorbitant-interest law (2003)
instruments.title: Tamil Nadu Prohibition of Charging Exorbitant Interest Act, 2003
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Any person lending money in Tamil Nadu
key_concepts: Exorbitant interest includes daily, hourly, kandhu and meter vatti and thandal, each defined by reference to a rate above that fixed under s. 7 of the Tamil Nadu Money-lenders Act (s. 2)
core_obligations: s. 3: charge no exorbitant interest on any loan
consequences_stated: s. 4: charging exorbitant interest or molesting a debtor to recover a loan, imprisonment up to three years and fine up to Rs 30,000
s. 5: a debtor may deposit the amount due with interest at the Government rate in court and seek an order recording satisfaction; the court may order restoration of property forcibly taken (s. 6)

instruments.short_name: Gujarat Money-Lenders Act 2011
instruments.title: Gujarat Money-Lenders Act, 2011 (amended in 2015 and 2018)
instruments.theme: Consumer protection and State lending laws
applies_to: Money-lenders carrying on business in Gujarat, registered with the district Registrar
key_concepts: No money-lender may carry on business except in the area and on the terms of its registration (s. 5(1))
NBFCs registered with RBI are deemed registered under the Act, but must intimate their RBI registration to the concerned Registrar in the prescribed proforma (s. 5(2))

The Supreme Court has held that the Gujarat Act, like the Kerala Money Lenders Act, does not apply to NBFCs registered with and regulated by RBI, because Chapter III-B of the RBI Act is a complete code for them (Nedumpilli Finance Co. v. State of Kerala, 2022 INSC 545)

The State Government may fix maximum rates of interest for any local area or class of money-lending business, for secured and unsecured loans; an agreement for interest above those rates is invalid (s. 33)
core_obligations: s. 5(2): on its face, an RBI-registered NBFC lending in Gujarat must intimate its RBI registration to the Registrar (see the Supreme Court ruling above on whether the Act reaches RBI-regulated NBFCs)
s. 33: charge no interest above the maximum rates fixed by the State Government
consequences_stated: s. 40: molesting a debtor to recover a loan is punishable with imprisonment and fine, with minimum terms for first and repeat offences

instruments.short_name: Rajasthan Stamp Act 1998
instruments.title: Rajasthan Stamp Act, 1998 (replaces the Indian Stamp Act in Rajasthan, except for Union-list instruments)
applies_to: Lenders executing or holding loan and security documents in Rajasthan
key_concepts: The Indian Stamp Act, 1899 as adapted in Rajasthan is repealed, except for documents in entry 91 of the Union List (such as bills of exchange, cheques and promissory notes), which stay under the central Act (s. 91)

Mortgage deeds (Article 37): where possession is given, the duty on a conveyance for the amount secured; where it is not, the duty on a bond (Article 14) for the amount secured; collateral or substituted security where the principal security is duly stamped is charged separately
Agreements relating to deposit of title-deeds, pawn or pledge fall under Article 6, and further charges under Article 30
core_obligations: Stamp loan and security documents executed in Rajasthan under the Rajasthan schedule, not the central Schedule I
